1.pericope_label: Supplications for all men, for kings and all in authority

schools.summary: Begin with the connective, since it carries the argument: the detailed injunctions are issued in pursuance of the charge already laid down, so the first detail is that the congregation pray. Take "first of all" as primacy of importance rather than order of service. Do not spend the hour dividing the four terms; give the working distinctions — a request for a particular benefit, the general word for prayer, a drawing near into free speech with God, and gratitude, the one form that outlasts the rest — and move on. Then supply the history the text assumes: Josephus on the refusal to pray for Roman magistrates, Tertullian's and Polycarp's testimony that the charge was kept, and the fact that the kings in view included Nero. Close on the last word, better rendered gravity or decorum than honesty.

Preach it as pastoral care rather than as polity. The one who leads is the common father of all the world, so his prayer must reach as far as God's own care. Draw the two effects out plainly: no one can hate the man he prays for, and those prayed for are made gentler by it — then press the hard case, what it meant for persecutors to learn that those they scourged were praying for them. Use the image of the father struck in the face by the child he carries and losing nothing of his affection. Answer the objection that "all men" means only the faithful by pointing at the kings, and note that the wider phrase stands first so the charge cannot be read as flattery of power.

Take the objection head on before expounding anything: why should we be anxious about the salvation of unbelievers? The command exists precisely to refuse that limit, and the congregation is to include those who at present have no connection with it. On the four words, do not manufacture precision the text does not supply; say honestly what can and cannot be distinguished, refuse the ceremonial construction some have put on them, and treat the heaping of terms as a goad to a duty at which we are all sluggish. Then handle the rulers concretely: these were enemies and persecutors, and the apostle enjoins prayer for them against a practice of cursing the nations and praying for none but one's own.

Open with what prayer is, not what it does: the vehemence of holy zeal and the ardour of divine love arising from a calm and undisturbed soul. Then set the fourfold division to work — averting evils, obtaining needed good, pleading for others, and thanks — and say plainly that this is a direction for the public assembly, offered for heathens as well as Christians and for enemies as well as friends. Bring in the ancient testimonies to show the practice was kept, from Cyprian before the proconsul to Tertullian's petition for a faithful senate and an obedient people. End on the magistrate: even the lowest of them does much good or much harm, which is reason enough to pray.

Make the scope the doctrine. See how far this religion was from being a sect, when it taught men to pray not only for those of their own way but for all. Note that no form is prescribed, only heads, so the liberty of prayer is left where the Spirit put it. On the rulers, grant frankly that they were heathens and persecutors, and say we must pray for them though we ourselves suffer under them. Then guard the petition from ambition: he does not say that we may grow rich or be in honour under them, but that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life — and remind the hearers that we cannot expect to be kept quiet unless we keep in all godliness and honesty.

debates.question: How are the four terms for prayer to be distinguished?

sides.position: Supplication is a request for a particular benefit and a species of the general word for prayer; intercession is a drawing near into free and familiar speech with God; thanksgiving is the form that alone survives in heaven
Four distinct acts: averting evils of every kind, obtaining the good things we need, pleading on behalf of others, and praising God for mercies received

The difference between three of the four is not thoroughly understood; the ceremonial construction put upon them is childish, and the heaping of words is meant to rouse a duty at which we are sluggish
Supplication is imploring help in time of need, prayer any offering up of our desires, intercession prayer for others; true prayer is the vehemence of holy zeal from a calm soul

debates.question: Why is prayer for rulers enjoined, and what is its object?

sides.position: That their wise rule may secure peace, and that the constant repetition of such prayer may stamp out all thought of revolt among the worshippers themselves
Because so much depends on their character and plans, and God has power to incline their hearts; the Christian asks only not to be harassed in the enjoyment of his religion
Because their safety is our security, and government is appointed by God for the public good; the rulers are a sort of bulwark within which those enclosed are at peace
Because it is for the public good that there be civil government, and we must pray for them though we ourselves suffer under them
Because even the lowest country magistrate frequently does much good or much harm

outliers.note: Alone makes the one who leads the common father of all the world, and alone draws out the two effects of praying for enemies -- that hatred is done away, since no one can hate the man he prays for, and that those prayed for lose their ferocity; his image is a father struck in the face by the child he carries, who loses nothing of his affection.

Alone supplies the external testimony that the charge was kept, quoting the Apology of Tertullian on intercession for the emperors and Polycarp's charge to pray for persecutors and cruel enemies, and alone cites Josephus on the refusal to pray for Roman magistrates that helped bring on the war.
Alone argues from the exhortation itself against a prescribed liturgy, reasoning that a bishop who had written the petitions would have no occasion to urge his presbyters to offer them.

themes: I exhort therefore, that, first of all, supplications, prayers, intercessions, and giving of thanks, be made for all men
For kings, and for all that are in authority; that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty

3.pericope_label: God our Saviour will have all men to be saved

schools.summary: This is where the sermon has to be careful, and the care is exegetical before it is doctrinal. Show that the verb of willing is not the verb of decree: what God wills in that sense is done, so this must denote desire, or what accords with his nature, as he wills that sickness be relieved and the oppressed go free. Refuse the escape that "all men" means some of every rank, and give the reasons — the plain sense, the unrestricted prayer commanded above for which this is the stated ground, and the unrestricted reasons that follow. Then set the limit the other way: the will is not to save all, or all would be saved, but that all should be saved, redemption universal yet conditional. Note that the word for knowledge is the full one.

Preach the will as effectual or not at all. What is willed here is no bare possibility, no offer, no placing of men in a salvable state, but a real and actual salvation, determined beforehand and made certain by God's own appointment, by the covenant, and by the mission that accomplished it. Press the alternative: a will hanging on man's performance could leave every man unsaved, and any who were saved would be saved of him that willeth, which Scripture denies. Do not let the hearers rest in a divided will, antecedent and consequent. On the opening verse, keep the point that prayer for enemies and persecutors is good in itself and in the sight of one who does not see as man sees, and is accepted only through Christ.

State the doctrine without hedging and let the text carry it: he wills seriously that all be saved, not a part only and much less the smallest part, and therefore he wills that all be prayed for. Ask the congregation the blunt question — in the face of such a declaration, how can any Christian soul suppose that God ever unconditionally and eternally reprobated any man? Then close the door on fatalism from the other side: those who come to the knowledge of the truth are not compelled, for the word means acknowledgment, the receiving of the truth as the rule of faith and the model of the life. Finish with the practical edge: if we ask why more are not converted, the answer is that we do not pray enough.

debates.question: In what sense does God will that all men be saved?

sides.position: Not as an absolute decree, which would certainly take effect, but as a desire agreeable to his nature; he has made provision, uses proper means, and if men are not saved the fault is their own
Not a will to save all, or all would be saved, but a will that all should be saved; through Christ's death all are rendered capable of salvation, redemption being universal yet conditional
A real, certain and actual salvation determined beforehand and secured by appointment, covenant and mission; not conditional, for then none might be saved

He wills the salvation of all seriously, not a part only and much less the smallest part; to suppose any man unconditionally and eternally reprobated is to know neither the nature of God nor the bowels of Christ
God's wish and will so far as he can influence men

debates.question: What is meant by coming to the knowledge of the truth?

sides.position: The full knowledge, the intellectual apprehension of Christianity, guarded against those who would lead the people astray
Acknowledgment: that the truth be proclaimed, and when heard, received as the rule of faith and the model of the life
Not the merely theoretical but the practical and saving truth as revealed in the gospel
The knowledge which brings salvation, and to which men are not compelled

outliers.note: Alone sets out three grounds for refusing the reading that all men means some of every rank and class: that it strains the obvious sense, that the prayer commanded above is for mankind without exception and this is given as its reason, and that the reasons which follow are unlimited in the same way.
Alone turns the verse into a rebuke of the praying church rather than an argument about the decree, answering the question why more are not converted with the reply that we do not pray enough.

themes: For this is good and acceptable in the sight of God our Saviour
Who will have all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge of the truth

5.pericope_label: One God, one mediator, who gave himself a ransom for all

schools.summary: Let the singulars do the preaching. One God is the regular Pauline premise for a universal gospel; one Mediator means there is not one for kings and another for their subjects, one for the rich and another for the poor, one for the master and another for the slave. Give the philology where it pays: the noun is a late word for a middle man, and the word for ransom joins a prefix of exchange to a preposition of substitution, so that both ideas stand in it. On the human nature named here, show why it is named — the Mediator must have taken it before he could suffer the death that was the ransom, and the mention silently refuses any teaching that the crucified was a phantom. On the testimony clause, say only that witness was to be borne in its own times.

Read the unity toward men rather than as a bare statement about the divine essence, or the verse will not carry the argument it is given to carry: one Creator, one providential preserver, one covenant God of Jew and Gentile alike, and therefore all sorts of men are to be prayed for. Then hold the ransom to its own logic. It was himself he gave, body and soul and life, into the hands of justice, in the room of those he redeemed. Grant the word "all" and deny that it means every individual, and give the reason plainly: were the price paid for each, each would be freed, or else God receives a sufficient satisfaction and still refuses to release the captive, which cannot be said of him.

Build the argument in steps and let the hearers count them: there is one God; he is the Creator of all; he has made his kindness known to all; he wills all to be saved; and he has provided one Mediator, who gave himself a ransom for all. Then say the conclusion outright — as surely as God created all men, so surely Christ died for all. Explain the ransom as an exchange in kind, a like or an equal given, life for life, and add that the dignity of the person redeeming made it more than equivalent to all mankind. Use the one Mediator against every other, whether the saints of a corrupt Christendom or the many mediators the heathen set up to pacify their superior gods, and end on the duty of publishing the testimony to every nation.

debates.question: How far does the ransom for all extend?

sides.position: To every human soul, for as surely as God created all men, so surely Christ died for all
To all, and this is itself the proof that God desires the salvation of all; whatever it proves for any of the race it proves for all
To all mankind, the price of redemption, his life in exchange for their forfeited lives
Not to every individual of mankind, for then all would be delivered and saved; otherwise the price is paid in vain, or God receives satisfaction and still refuses to free the captive
Such a ransom as gives a like or an equal, life for life, and from the dignity of the person redeeming more than equivalent to all mankind

debates.question: What is the testimony borne in its own times?

sides.position: That the truth would be made known through all the world at the proper season, not having been fully known under the ancient dispensation
The death itself was the witness to the truth of the offering made in the eternal counsels
The doctrine reserved for its own times, to be delivered in due course to every nation, as the versions and the older translators variously render it
His own seasons, chosen by his own wisdom
A testimony in its due seasons, standing in apposition to the preceding clause without predicate or participle

outliers.note: Alone presses the one Mediator into a social argument, that there is not one for kings and another for their subjects, one for the rich and another for the poor, one for the master and another for the slave, so that a servant may know himself regarded with the same interest as his owner.

Alone canvasses the text of the testimony clause at length, setting the printed Vulgate beside the renderings of Macknight, Wakefield and Rosenmueller, reporting a single Cambridge manuscript that reads mystery for testimony, and tracing how the reading printed under one pope was corrected under the next.
Alone reads the mention of the Mediator's manhood as a silent refutation of the docetic error that the figure nailed to the cross was no man but a phantom.

themes: For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus
Who gave himself a ransom for all, to be testified in due time
Whereunto I am ordained a preacher, and an apostle... a teacher of the Gentiles in faith and verity

8.pericope_label: That men pray everywhere, lifting up holy hands

schools.summary: Note the change of verb: this is the milder word, a willingness rather than the active volition used of God's will above, and yet it carries apostolic authority. Explain "in every place" against the assumption it displaces, that prayer had a privileged address at the temple, and let the words to the woman of Samaria stand behind it. On the lifted hands, give the evidence from Jewish practice and from the early Christians, note that they stood to pray, and take "holy" as hands undefiled. Reserve the weight for the last two words. The one rendered doubting runs from reckoning through reasoning to debate; take it of clamorous contention, and make the application to those who dispute for victory and then cannot pray together.

The congregation will hear a contradiction here, so answer it first: Christ said to shut the door and pray in secret, and this says pray everywhere. The command was against ostentation, not about geography — the same Lord who said let not the left hand know what the right does was regulating vainglory, not hands. Then draw the contrast the apostle intends, between Christian prayer and a worship confined to one temple in one city. Having freed the place, tighten the manner. Ask what holy hands are, and answer that they are not hands washed with water but hands free from covetousness and rapacity, hands employed in almsgiving. Take the last word as misgiving, and press the promise that what is asked believing is received.

Make the authority plain at the outset: he speaks nothing but what he received, so his "I will" is a command. Then keep "everywhere" from becoming an abstraction. Trace how the Jews narrowed prayer to the temple, then to the land, then to the oratories built by rivers and the sea, and answer that all places belong to God's dominion; give them the maxim to carry home, that a praying heart will always find a praying place. On the lifted hands, take the gesture back to the laying of hands on the offering, so that the worshipper comes to the altar and lays his hand on the Lamb. Define wrath widely — against any creature, and every motion of the soul that is not according to love — and name the three hindrances: wrath, unholy action, and want of faith.

Keep this short and let it be a list the hearers can use. Under the gospel prayer is not confined to any one house of prayer: pray in the closet, in the family, at meals, on journeys, and in the assemblies, whether more public or private. Then the two conditions, and no more than two. Pray in charity, without wrath or malice or anger at any person; and pray in faith, without doubting and without disputing. The doctrine is that the extent of the duty matches the extent of the places — wherever men are, there prayer should be.

Explain why only men are named without letting the hearers draw more from the silence than it holds. It is public prayer in the church that is in view, and leading it belongs to the men; prayer in the house and the closet is as much the duty and the privilege of women. Set the phrase "in every place" against the rule that prayer offered away from Jerusalem had still to be directed toward it, and say that the hour the Lord spoke of has now come. Then carry the conditions over from the previous verse rather than inventing new ones: purity of heart and hand, without murmuring toward God, without wrath toward others, and in faith without distrust.

debates.question: What does the word rendered doubting mean?

sides.position: Not doubt of one's own piety but clamorous disputing; the word runs from reckoning through reasoning to debate, and men heated for victory are unfit to pray together
Disputing: the religious contentions among the believers themselves
Reasonings, the controversy of faith and unbelief in the bosom of a distressed penitent or timid believer, in which unbelief ordinarily triumphs
That which is contrary to faith, one of the three grand hindrances to God's hearing our petitions
Misgiving as to whether we shall be heard at all

debates.question: How does praying everywhere agree with the command to pray in secret?

sides.position: The command in the Gospel was against ostentation, not about place; the apostle's object is to distinguish Christian from Jewish prayer, which was bound to one temple
The Jews supposed special efficacy at the temple and the heathen at their shrines; Christianity teaches that God may be worshipped in any place
It answers a Jewish rule that narrowed prayer to Jerusalem, then to the land, then to the oratories; all places belong to God's dominion, and a praying heart will find a praying place
It fulfils the word spoken to the woman of Samaria, that worship would be bound neither to that mountain nor to Jerusalem

outliers.note: Alone quotes at length the passage on anger as a hindrance to prayer -- the lark beaten back by the loud sighings of an eastern wind until the storm is over -- and alone applies the verse to theologians so heated by debate that they are in no state of mind to pray together.

Alone refers the lifted hands to the laying of hands on the head of a sin offering, so that the worshipper comes to the altar, lays his hand on the Lamb, and by faith offers it in his own behalf, and alone cites the rabbinic permission of ejaculatory prayer standing, sitting, leaning, lying, walking and at labour.

Alone harmonises the command to pray everywhere with the command to enter the closet and shut the door, holding that the latter regulated ostentation and not location, since the same Lord who said let not the left hand know what the right does was not speaking of hands.

themes: I will therefore that men pray every where, lifting up holy hands, without wrath and doubting

9.pericope_label: Women in modest apparel, adorned with good works

schools.summary: Establish the setting before the application, because everything turns on it: the verb of willing carries over from the previous verse and the subject is still the conduct of public worship. Then refuse to quarantine the principle there — if a manner of dress is fitting in the sanctuary it is fitting anywhere. Use the verb "adorn" to keep the sermon honest: ornament as such is not condemned, since the world God made is full of beauty and every flower shows he is not against decoration; the quarrel is over what true ornament is. Give the rule that can actually be applied: the line is crossed when the outward decoration occupies the mind more than the virtues of the heart. Add that negligence offends as truly as excess, and end where the text ends, on good works.

Read the list as a list and do not soften it: braided hair, gold, pearls, costly array are named expressly to women professing godliness, with no exception offered, and no art of man reconciles the wilful breach of an express command with the profession. Then give the reason underneath the rule, that where much time and cost go on decorating the person it is painful evidence of little within. Furnish the historical picture — the plain long garment and the mantle over it, modest as any dress ever devised, and the extravagance that overlaid them with gold and precious stones. Close with the Jewish matrons calling to the bride that she needed no paint, no antimony, no braided hair, being most beautiful herself.

Preach it as a matter of the heart read off the habit: you may read the vanity of a person's mind in the gaudiness of the dress. Say that those who profess godliness should dress as becomes their profession, and put the alternative in terms of money — what is laid out on fine clothes could be laid out in works of piety and charity. Make good works the best ornament, and add that they are in the sight of God of great price. Two observations are worth drawing: that the rules of this religion reach not only to the person but to the dress and the deportment, and that women profess godliness as well as men, being baptized and thereby engaged to it.

Set the order first: let the women pray likewise, not leading and not serving as the mouth of the church, which would be indecent, but joining in the public prayer with the same purity of heart and hand required of the men, without murmuring toward God and without distrust. Then take the dress as the subject it is, the clothing proper to the hour of prayer and to any part of public worship. On the profession named at the close, do not narrow it: it is not merely the fear of God, nor internal religion alone, nor the form of godliness, nor outward holiness of life, but the whole of religion inward and outward, professed at baptism and still held.

debates.question: How strictly are the four ornaments forbidden?

sides.position: Expressly and by name to all women professing godliness, with no exception; no art of man can reconcile the wilful violation of an express command with the Christian profession

Mere braiding is not forbidden, nor all use of gold or pearls; no exact rule can be given, since much depends on age, rank and means, and the line is passed when the outward occupies the mind more than the heart
What is forbidden is the conspicuous dress or showy ornament likely to draw attention and distract fellow worshippers at divine service
Not the custom or costume of the country, which may be followed, but the extravagance of those who deck themselves to attract admiration and flattery

debates.question: What does the word rendered modest apparel denote?

sides.position: That which is well-ordered, decorous and becoming, rather than the opposite of immodest

The outer garment itself, the mantle worn loose over the long robe of Greece and Rome; though a contrary opinion is reported, that no article of dress is meant at all but the government of the mind over dress and demeanour alike
Neatness of apparel joined to modesty of demeanour, the inward shrinking from anything unbecoming

outliers.note: Alone argues from the verb adorn that ornament as such is not condemned, since the world as God made it is full of beauty and every flower shows he is not opposed to decoration, and alone warns that a negligent appearance violates the precept as truly as excess does.

Alone reconstructs the garments themselves, the long robe girded beneath the breast and the mantle gathered at the shoulder, notes which openings marked an immodest wearer, and alone brings in Homer's Euphorbus, whose ringlets bound about with twine of gold and silver swept the dust.
Alone points beyond this passage to the graver reason for modest demeanour alleged elsewhere, because of the angels.

themes: In like manner also, that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety
But (which becometh women professing godliness) with good works

11.pericope_label: Let the woman learn in silence; Adam first formed; saved in childbearing

schools.summary: Handle the two grounds separately, since they are two. On the first, deny that bare priority of existence is the argument — that would give every older person authority over a younger — and put the weight on the account itself, the woman formed from the man's side and given as a companion. On the second, be candid that the readings differ: whether the compounded verb marks Eve as thoroughly deceived over against the simple verb used of Adam is disputed, and the philology will not settle it. On the closing promise, lay the options out by name before choosing, and if you reject the reading that finds the Incarnation in "the childbearing," say why; if you keep it, say what it does and does not prove. It is fair to admit, as one of this school does, that something here seems left unexpressed.

Do not preach beyond the text into a general theory. The prohibition is of public teaching; say that, and refer the hearers to the fuller treatment elsewhere rather than settling the whole question here. Where a reason is wanted, give the sources their own words: the frame fitted for public exertion, the sentence of Genesis, and the ancient line that nature does not grant a woman rule — and let the hearer weigh them. On the last verse, take the promise as spoken to the sex generally, carried safe through the pain and danger the sentence entails and finally saved if they continue in loving faith and holy wisdom. Then shut a door: the act of bearing children entitles no one to anything, for pain neither purifies nor makes atonement, and faith, love and holiness are as needful for every daughter of Eve as for every son of Adam.

Divide the ban exactly where the text divides it. Teaching in the church is an act of authority and is withheld; teaching in the house is commanded, and the mother's doctrine is no more to be forsaken than the father's — Timothy himself is the standing example, taught by his mother and his grandmother. Then take the second reason at full strength and without the usual softenings: the man was not deceived at all, neither by the serpent, with whom he never spoke, nor by his wife; he knew what he took and what would follow, and ate out of fondness for her, that she might not die alone. Draw the conclusion that follows — sinning knowingly and against light, his sin was the greater — and let the last verse be comfort, not condition.

Preach the silence as order rather than as a penalty, and preach it to the room you are standing in. The regulation runs on from dress to speech because both are about the same thing. Say plainly what the rule requires, and then say what has become of it: they talk here more than in the market or at the bath, as though they had come for recreation, and while our discourse strains against the noise nobody learns anything useful. Put the promise at the end where it belongs — that this quiet will adorn her more than any garments, and that so clothed she will be able to offer her prayers in the manner most becoming.

debates.question: How far does the prohibition of teaching reach?

sides.position: To public ministration and to questioning in the assembly; teaching those of one's own sex privately was afterwards expressly allowed and required of deaconesses
To the church only; women may and should teach in their own houses and families, as Timothy was taught by his mother and grandmother
To anything, public or private, that belongs to man as his peculiar function, as the Roman law also removed women from every public office
To public teaching
To speaking at all in the church, even about spiritual things; this is order, this is modesty, and it adorns more than any garment
Clearly to the public meeting; and yet all modern Christians allow women to teach classes, so something seems not to be expressed here that would make it clear

debates.question: In what sense was Adam not deceived?

sides.position: Both sinned, but only Eve was deluded; the compounded verb conveys thoroughness, and weakness in the understanding is the very sinew of the argument
It is not certain that the compound means completely deceived in contrast to the simple verb used of Adam
Not merely that he was not deceived first: he was never deceived at all, having never conversed with the serpent, and ate knowingly out of fondness for his wife, so that his sin was the greater
He was not deceived by the serpent nor first in the transgression; the woman opposed a feebler resistance, though in many traits she is the superior
The serpent deceived Eve; Eve did not deceive Adam but persuaded him. She is more easily deceived and more easily deceives
Satan did not attempt the man; Adam took the fruit from his wife's hand knowing he transgressed, but she led the way, and in consequence was subjected to his rule

debates.question: What is meant by being saved in childbearing?

sides.position: That the way of salvation stands open to her on the same terms as to man even under the sentence of sorrow; the messianic reading is too refined, is not the plain sense of the word, and would not save her in any case
Through the bringing forth of the Saviour: the sex is saved by the childbearing of a woman, since safety in travail plainly does not follow faith and holiness
The article gives the clue: through THE childbearing, the Incarnation, by the relation in which woman stood to the Messiah
That translation is true, but the emphasis falls on childbearing as the peculiar function of woman with a dignity of its own; she is saved in it, not by means of it
Women in general are carried safe through the pain and danger the sentence entails, and finally saved if they continue in loving faith and holy wisdom

outliers.note: Alone follows the rule forward into church history, noting that when the prohibition was renewed at Carthage the same council expressly permitted women to teach others of their own sex in private, and that the ability to instruct ignorant and rustic women was required as a qualification in deaconesses.

Alone admits the difficulty out loud, observing that modern Christians allow women to teach classes and that something seems not to be expressed here that would make it all clear, and alone traces the disputed verb to a vernacular word for playing the master that survives in the modern Greek title of respect.

Alone sets the injunction beside Roman law, quoting the Pandects to the effect that women were precluded from all public offices and could not be judges, execute the function of magistrates, sue, plead or act as proxies.

Alone catalogues the competing readings of the closing promise by name -- the whole of the maternal calling, the training of children, preservation from the impostors and luxury of the age, and the messianic sense -- before choosing among them.

themes: Let the woman learn in silence with all subjection
For Adam was first formed, then Eve
Notwithstanding she shall be saved in childbearing, if they continue in faith and charity and holiness with sobriety
